permission.description: Reports the engine's base URL and boot token to the main window. With the token, every engine route is reachable (docs/00 §6.3), so this permission is the reason the local-origin bypass below had to be closed.
Reports whether the engine process is up, without starting it.

Returns the tail of the engine's own stderr. Read-only and bounded (200 lines, 500 characters each), and the engine is the only writer: this is the explanation for an engine that stopped, not a way to run anything.
Lists the eight role slots and their per-role configuration, with API keys redacted (docs/00 §6.4).
Writes one role's configuration. Read-modify-write over the same key, so a lost race is a lost update rather than a credential leak.
Restores missing or malformed role slots to their defaults. Destructive to local state by design, so it is granted explicitly rather than swept in by a wildcard.
Probes a provider connection and reports the failure, without persisting anything.
Starts a PTY the user asked for. A terminal is arbitrary code execution by another name, so the grant names it rather than inheriting it.
Writes keystrokes to an existing PTY.
Resizes an existing PTY so the shell redraws to fit.
Closes an existing PTY.

Opens a machine: a jailed shell on a registered workspace, which the assistant may also type into. The window chooses whether it has a network, once, here; nothing afterwards can change it, and there is no fallback to an unjailed shell.
Types into one machine, by its own id. A terminal's id is refused: machines are a separate registry.
Resizes one machine's pseudo-terminal so output wraps at its pane's width.
Closes a machine and ends everything running in its jail.
Opens a browser webview. The webview itself holds no permission (capabilities/browser.json is empty), so this grants the *main window* the ability to open one — it does not grant that page anything.
Navigates an existing browser page, through the same loopback guard as `open`.

Shows one browser page and hides the others. Visibility is the stacking order for embedded pages; this grants the *main window* the switch, and grants a browser page nothing — it cannot even show itself.
Resizes every browser page to the rectangle the UI measured. Geometry comes from the UI's own layout, never from a page.
Closes a browser webview by tab id.

Opens a browser page's DevTools inspector. A shell-side surface over the webview — it grants the page nothing; a browser page cannot even open its own inspector. Built with the devtools feature; the command is compiled out without it.
Closes a browser page's DevTools inspector.
Reports whether this build has a DevTools inspector at all. Compile-time metadata, so the UI asks the shell instead of hardcoding the build shape.
Reports whether a browser page's DevTools inspector is open. Read-only, and the reason the pane's control can show the real state instead of guessing.

set.description: Every command this app defines, as twenty-four named permissions and no wildcard. The point of listing them one by one is that a command added to `invoke_handler!` without a line here does not become reachable — it is stripped from the handler at compile time, and src-tauri/src/browser/ fails the build's test leg if the two lists ever differ. Permissions are not where a webview is decided: this set is referenced only by capabilities/default.json, whose `webviews` is `["main"]`, and capabilities/browser.json keeps an empty list for `browser-*`.
